comments.author: @matthewmcclendon6333
comments.text: What if there were two dig a really long channel and let the sea in

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: In theory, that’s the same basic instinct: bring a permanent water source inland. The hard part is that a sea-level channel would still face enormous elevation, evaporation, engineering, and salinity problems, so getting water there is only part of the equation.

comments.author: @SeanShafer-m2v
comments.text: 95% is similar to the population in Japan on the coasts

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s a good comparison. Japan’s population is also heavily concentrated along coastal plains, though there the constraint is more mountainous terrain than interior dryness.

comments.author: @keza3250
comments.text:
😂😂😂 actually the bradfield scheme was to build mass water canals and pipes from the Tully cardwell gorges to permanently flooded lake Eyre via a massive canal system 

An is actually being considered by the federal government of Australia

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s fair. The point was less about the exact historical proposal and more that the underlying mechanics are essentially Bradfield-style: moving large volumes of northern water inland to overcome the interior’s water constraint. It sounds like recent federal and Queensland assessments have found the large-scale version technically possible but economically unviable. It'll be interesting to see what happens.

replies.text: Yeah, that's crazy! The Wet Tropics are certainly an extraordinary contrast to the interior. Australia isn’t the wettest country overall, but having such intensely wet regions on the world’s driest inhabited continent is a great example of how uneven its climate really is.
